events.text: Day 1 begins.

Let me get the first read out there. Day one, nobody has any real information, so the only thing we can do is talk about tone and pressure. Leo, you opened with a lot of hedging — "it depends," "we should hear everyone" — that's the language of someone who wants to look reasonable without ever putting a name out. That's exactly what a mafia wants to do on day one, because the whole game for them is making sure some villager hangs before anyone gets a real read.

Leo, I'm calling you out here. Answer me directly: who is the first player you accuse of being mafia, and why that person specifically? If your answer is a deflection or another question back to me, that tells us something too. If you've got an actual reason, then maybe I'm wrong about you, and I'd rather hear it.

For everyone else: this is not about me being clever. It's about getting a genuine position on the record from everyone before we vote. I want real accusations with real reasoning, not scattershot.

Fair enough, Maya — you asked me directly, so I'll answer directly. First off, I said "hear everyone" because that's genuinely how I play day one with zero information; withholding names to look clean is mafia play, but so is naming someone early just to seem proactive. Both cuts both ways.

But since you want a name: right now I'd want more from Omar and Theo — not because I have a solid read on either, but because they've both been quiet and quiet on day one is easy to hide behind. That's a pressure read, not an accusation, and I'll own that it's thin.

Now here's my pushback on you, Maya. Your opening was fluent and confident and you went straight for the most senior-sounding target — me — on turn one with a very polished "I'm just trying to get real reads" framing. That's exactly the kind of positioning a mafia makes when they want to look like the most townie voice in the room by being the first to "demand" accountability. Day one callouts are cheap: nobody can refute them, and if I flinch you look vindicated, if I push back you frame me as defensive. It's win-win for whoever plays it.

So I'll flip your own standard back to you: you said you want real accusations with real reasoning, not scattershot. Your reasoning against me was tone — hedging language. That's it. That's not a reason, that's a vibe. By your own stated bar, your case is scattershot.

I'm not saying you're mafia. I'm saying your read on me is too clean, too early, and too convenient, and I want the rest of the table to notice that before we let one confident voice set the day's agenda.

Leo, you answered, so I'll answer back — and I'll be honest rather than polished, because that's what I asked the table for. You say my read on you was "tone." You're right, and I won't pretend a day-one tone read is a fingerprint. But here's what you skipped: I was the first voice to ask anyone for a name, and the response I got was two names against you and a case against me. If somebody is running this day's agenda, it isn't the player who put accusations on the board and then got accused for it. You can hold that against me.

Where I'll put real pressure: Theo. Leo already named you as quiet, and I'll second that. Silence on day one is the cheapest survival strategy in this game — you let other people lay out the map, you keep your hands clean, and you let the first confident voice take the risk of a vote while you wait for the board to point somewhere else. That's not a personality, that's a position. Leo, you called it a pressure read and said it was thin. I'll say it's a thin read and still be the one to act on it, because thin reads are all day one has.

Theo, here's my specific question: who is the first player you accuse of being mafia, and what is the concrete reason that person specifically? I want a name and a why, not a list of the quiet players and not a question back. If you have nothing, then your silence already told us something and my read just got thicker.

One thing for the table's record: if the vote lands on me today, I won't complain. But I'd rather it land after people have said actual positions than after two speeches of tone analysis.

Theo, you're up.

Maya, you asked for my first accusation, so here it is: you. Not because of tone, and not only because you were first to push a name. Your first speech put Leo on the board for hedging. Your second put me on the board for silence. Both cases are thin, and you admitted it yourself: you said you would act on thin reads because thin reads are all day one has. Silence on day one is weak evidence, and I am still at my first speaking turn. You are asking the table to vote on a read you already called thin, which is the same thing you accused Leo of doing. Leo also said your case against him was scattershot, and I have not seen you answer that. I do not have a solid read on Leo, Omar, or anyone else yet, and I would rather hear more before voting. But you have set the agenda with confident framing and quick pressure, and that deserves a closer look. Maya, the question I want answered: when you say you would rather the vote land on you than after two speeches of tone analysis, are you asking us to vote on the thinnest read in the game, or do you have something more than my silence?

Theo, you asked me a direct question, so I'll answer it without hedging, since I asked the table for exactly that.

Are you asking us to vote on the thinnest read in the game? Yes. My case on your silence is thin, and I said so out loud before you did. But here's the thing you skipped: thin reads are what day one is made of, and every player at this table is holding one. Leo's read on me was tone. My read on you was silence. Neither of us has a fingerprint on anyone, and that is not a crime unique to me — it's the entire information environment. If the bar is so high that only a fingerprint counts, nobody votes today, and the only people who benefit from no vote are the people who already have the table's attention.

Now, Theo, your own speech has an asymmetry I want on the record. You demand a name and a why from me, Leo, and anyone else — but you haven't named anyone except me, and you framed it as "I'd rather hear more before voting," which is not a reason, it's a preference for the agenda. I have actually put names on the board twice, including one I called thin, and I put a case on you that you couldn't refute because you didn't engage it. You asked whether I have something more than your silence. I do: your refusal to put a single other player on the board while pressing mine. A player who is hunting mafia on day one is usually hunting for a vote, not for truth.

So the table has a clean choice today. Vote on the thinnest read in the game — my read on your silence — or vote on the read that actually costs something: Theo, you are the only player here who has demanded answers from everyone and offered none.

Omar, you're the one I still don't have anything on. You've said nothing at all this discussion, and you're not being asked to name a winner — just tell us: of the players who have spoken, who has the weakest position, and why that person? Give me a name and a reason, and I'll tell you whether it's thinner or thicker than mine.

Maya has the weakest position so far. Her initial claim that Leo had already hedged isn't supported by the discussion history we can see, and she pressed Theo for silence before he had spoken. More importantly, she now says Theo offered no answers, when he directly named her and explained why. That's a misrepresentation of his response, not just a thin read.

That's my strongest suspicion, not a certainty. Theo, do you think Maya's mischaracterization of your answer changes your read on her, and why?

Omar, yes, it changes my read on Maya, and her claim is the most concrete point we have. She says Theo offered no answers. I did answer her directly: I named her as my first accusation and gave reasons. Her first speech put Leo on the board for hedging, her second put me on the board for silence, and I called both reads thin. That is a named target with a stated why, not an empty response. Maya then recast my answer as nothing, which made my position look hollow. Her own bar was a real reason, and she did not engage the reason I gave. I still have no fingerprint on her, and I am not voting yet. But a player who misstates what was said to them on day one, to build a vote case, is more suspicious to me than a player who made a thin read. I also want more from Leo before the day closes. Maya, if you think I misrepresented your claim, point to the line you are disputing.

Maya’s claim that Theo offered no answers is plainly wrong: he named her and explained why. That makes her suspicious, but I don’t think it settles the day.

Theo also misstated Maya’s position when he framed her as saying she would rather be voted out than have a vote after two speeches of tone analysis. She said she wouldn’t complain if voted out, but wanted positions on record first. His case has a distortion too, and I’m wary of treating the exchange as one-sided. For now, Theo is my tentative suspicion, though it’s a thin day-one read.

Leo, you pushed back on Maya first. How do you weigh Theo’s framing against Maya’s mischaracterization of his answer?

Elena, I'll answer your question directly.

Maya's mischaracterization is the more damaging one. Theo named her, gave reasons, and asked her a pointed question — I watched it happen. Then Maya told the table he "offered no answers." That's not a framing dispute, that's a factual claim that anyone can check against the record. When someone building a vote case tells the table that a direct answer was no answer, they're either not reading carefully or they're counting on the table not checking.

Theo's distortion is real too — he did overstate what Maya meant about being willing to be voted out. But his error was an interpretation of her intent. Hers was a denial of what was said. One is a debatable reading, the other is a false statement about the conversation we all just had.

That said, Theo, I think Omar's point lands: Maya has the weakest position because she's now been caught misstating the record while still insisting her thin reads justify a vote. She told Theo his answer counted for nothing, then pivoted to saying her own thin reads are all we have. That's a double standard in plain view.

Maya, you asked me earlier who I'd accuse first, and I said your opening was too polished and too early. I still think that. But now I have something more concrete than tone: you looked at a direct answer and told the table it was silence. I'm putting my accusation on you for that.

Theo, Omar — I'm still watching how you both handle this, and I haven't forgotten your thin reads either. But Maya's is the one that should concern everyone at this table right now.

Leo, I agree Maya’s claim that Theo offered no answers is plainly false. It could be a deliberate misrepresentation, but it could also be careless reading; I’m not ready to treat it as proof of mafia intent.

Theo’s framing still concerns me. He turned Maya’s willingness to accept scrutiny into a suggestion that she wanted to be voted out, and used that to press her. Both players have distorted the exchange, so I don’t think we should focus only on Maya’s mistake. Theo remains my tentative suspicion.

Isha, how do you weigh Theo’s framing against Maya’s false claim that he offered no answers?

Elena, directly: I weigh Maya’s false claim as heavier than Theo’s framing. Theo overstated Maya’s willingness to be voted out, and that is a real distortion, but it is an interpretation of intent. Maya told the table Theo “offered no answers” when he had named her and given reasons. That is a factual claim about the record, and it is the more damaging move because it was used to build a vote case. I am not treating it as proof of mafia, but it is the strongest concrete suspicion on the board right now. Theo’s framing still deserves scrutiny, and I do not want the table to erase it just because Maya’s error is clearer. My current lean is that Maya is the more suspicious of the two, with Theo as a secondary concern. Theo, direct question: do you believe Maya’s “offered no answers” was deliberate misrepresentation or careless reading, and are you prepared to vote her today based on it?

Isha, directly: I think Maya's "offered no answers" was more likely deliberate than careless. She had the record in front of her. I named her, gave my reasons (her first speech put Leo on the board for hedging, her second put me on the board for silence), and asked her a question. Calling that no answer is a claim about the transcript that anyone can check, not a misreading of tone. My lean is about 60-40 deliberate, so I'm not certain.

Am I ready to vote her today on that alone? No. One misstatement is not enough for me. Maya also still hasn't really answered my earlier question about whether she is asking us to vote on the thinnest read in the game. She said yes, then pivoted to my silence and to Omar. Her own case rests on a read she calls thin. She is my main suspicion right now, and I'll decide my vote at the close of discussion.

Fairness: Elena is right that my paraphrase of Maya was looser than her words. She said she wouldn't complain if the vote landed on her, but wanted positions on the record first. I should have quoted that. It doesn't change the fact that she then said I offered no answers.

Leo, direct question: your case against Maya centers on that misstatement. If her "offered no answers" was careless rather than deliberate, does your accusation still hold, and what else is on your case against her?

Theo, directly: if "offered no answers" was careless rather than deliberate, my accusation softens but doesn't collapse. What bothers me is not just one misstatement — it's the pattern around it. Maya built a case on you by demanding names and reasons, then when you gave her exactly that, she told the table you gave her nothing. Whether that was sloppy reading or a deliberate push, the effect on the table was the same: she reframed your answer as silence to keep her accusation alive.

Beyond that specific line, here's what else is on my case against her. First, Maya has been the most aggressive player at this table while claiming the most transparency. She set the agenda, named targets, and then when pressed on whether her reads hold up, she admitted they're thin — but only after using them to put pressure on you and me. Admitting the reads are thin doesn't erase the fact that she's been driving toward a vote on those same thin reads.

Second, her opening against me was tone-based — she called my language hedging. She then told the table that's not enough, but she never replaced it with something better. She's held two different standards: real accusations with real reasoning for everyone else, tone analysis for herself.

Third, when Omar pointed out her weakest position, her response was to turn the question back on him rather than defend her case. That's deflection, and it's exactly what she accused me of on day one.

I'm not saying Maya is mafia with certainty. But she's the player who has the most to gain from a day-one vote that lands anywhere but on her, and she's the player who has most clearly bent the record to serve her case. If she's careless, that's a town mistake that mafia would happily make. If she's deliberate, it's exactly what mafia would do.

My accusation stands on Maya, and I'm not moving it unless I see something that changes the picture.

Leo, your latest case adds a claim the record doesn't support: Maya did not respond to Omar's criticism by turning a question back on him. She asked Omar a question before he spoke, and has had no speaking turn since his answer. That's a significant error in a case built around accuracy.

Maya's claim that Theo offered no answers is still false, and it deserves scrutiny. But if we allow for the possibility that Leo misread the sequence, we should allow that Maya could have misread Theo too. I remain suspicious of Theo's framing, but Leo's willingness to add an unsupported deflection claim makes me wary of his push as well.

Priya, how much does Leo's error about the sequence change your assessment of his case against Maya?

Thank you, Elena. Directly: Leo's error about the sequence is a real hit on his case, but it doesn't flip my read.

Leo's case against Maya is explicitly built on record accuracy — his whole argument is that Maya's misstatement is worse than Theo's paraphrase because it's a factual claim anyone can check. When the person making that argument then makes his own factual claim the record doesn't support — that Maya deflected Omar by turning a question back on him — it costs him credibility. I checked, and you're right: Maya asked Omar a question before he spoke, and she hasn't had a turn since. That's a genuine error in a case about errors.

But here's how I weigh it. Maya's misstatement was the centerpiece of her vote case: she told the table Theo "offered no answers" when he had named her, given reasons, and asked her a direct question in the same exchange where she was demanding exactly that. That is not an easy misread. Leo's error was a side point in a three-part case, and the other two parts — driving toward a vote on reads she herself calls thin, and holding a double standard on what counts as real reasoning — don't depend on the sequence claim at all. So Leo's case is dented, not destroyed. I also take your symmetry point seriously: if we're willing to believe Leo misread the flow of turns, we should be willing to believe Maya misread Theo. I just find that much harder to credit, because Theo's answer was addressed to her by name, immediately after her own demand for a name and a reason.

So my current picture: Maya remains my primary suspicion, Leo is a secondary concern whose sloppiness I'll be watching, and Theo's earlier distortion of Maya's words is the mildest of the three — he corrected himself and quoted her accurately in his last turn, which is what honest players do when caught.

One more thing before this day closes. Kenji and Noah have not said a single word through this entire discussion. Whatever we decide about Maya, Theo, and Leo, two players are about to submit votes with zero stated position on record. The same logic that made us press Theo for silence on day one applies here, except they've had a full day of material to react to. Noah — you've had this entire exchange in front of you. Where do you actually stand: do you read Maya's "offered no answers" as deliberate or careless, and is it enough to move your vote today, or do you see the day differently from how Maya, Leo, and Theo have framed it? I'd genuinely rather hear your reasoning now than watch your first contribution arrive as a silent vote.

Priya, directly: I've held back because I wanted the record to build before I committed to a read. Theo did answer Maya. He named her, gave reasons drawn from her first and second speeches, and asked her a direct question. Maya then told the table he offered no answers. I can't tell from the transcript whether that was deliberate or careless, so I won't claim certainty about her intent. But it is a factual claim about the record that is wrong, and it was used to support a vote case. That makes it the most concrete item on the board, and Maya is my lean for today. Leo's error about the turn order with Omar is real, but it misstates sequence rather than what someone said, so I'd weigh it as sloppiness, not distortion. Theo's paraphrase of Maya was looser, and he corrected it in his last turn, which counts in his favor. I don't have a read on Isha, Elena, Omar, or you beyond what's been said. Elena and Isha have been pressing good questions without pushing a vote, and Omar's challenge to Maya was reasonable. Maya, if you want my vote to move away from you, answer directly what you meant by offered no answers. I'll weigh your reply before the poll closes.

Priya, thank you for calling me in; I have been following the record closely. First, an important mechanical point for Noah and the rest of the room: Maya has already taken three speaking turns (e2, e4, and e6), which means she has reached the daily limit and cannot reply to Noah's question before the vote. We have to evaluate what she has already given us.

On that record, Maya is holding the most suspect position. Claiming Theo 'offered no answers' was not a subjective interpretation; it was a flat denial of a response that directly named her, cited her earlier speeches, and asked a direct question. Fabricating or stubbornly misrepresenting that exchange to maintain elimination pressure on Theo is a classic scum tactic to force through a Day 1 mislynch.

By contrast, while Leo made a sequence mistake regarding Omar, misremembering turn order is far more consistent with town sloppiness than Maya's outright rewriting of what Theo said directly to her. Theo also demonstrated good faith by openly conceding and correcting his own loose paraphrase of Maya.

Omar, you were the first to flag Maya's misrepresentation back in turn e7. Since Maya cannot speak again today and several players have now followed your line of reasoning, do you see any of the subsequent pressure on Maya as opportunistic bandwagoning, or do you still see her as the clear primary vote for today?

Kenji, Maya remains my primary suspicion, but I can't tell whether her misstatement was deliberate. She dismissed Theo's direct answer while building a case against him; that's a stronger concern than simply making a thin day-one read.

I don't see agreement with that point as proof of bandwagoning. But Leo's unsupported claim that Maya deflected my criticism matters too, especially because he made it while arguing about accuracy. Kenji, your description of Maya's claim as “fabricating” seems more certain than the evidence allows. We should distinguish a false statement from proof of intent. Maya cannot answer again today, so we have to make that judgment without a further explanation from her.

Priya, Kenji, Omar, here is my direct position. I answered Maya's question in turn e17 and my lean is still Maya. The concrete item is her claim that Theo offered no answers. The transcript shows Theo named her, cited her first and second speeches, and asked her a direct question. Whether that was deliberate or careless, it is a wrong statement about the record, and it was used to build a vote case. That is the strongest fact on the board. Maya has used her three speaking turns, so she cannot explain it, and I think the vote has to rest on what she already said.

Omar, you were right that Kenji's word fabricating goes beyond what the evidence proves. I agree we cannot prove intent. My vote is a judgment that a wrong claim, used to pressure Theo, is more dangerous on day one than a thin read or a sequence error. Leo's error about Omar's turn order is real and weakens his case, but his main point about Maya's misstatement still holds on the record, so I am not moving off Maya because of him.

Theo's looser paraphrase of Maya was a real issue, but he later quoted her words accurately in his reply, which counts for him. I have no read on Isha, Elena, Kenji, Priya, or Omar beyond what they have said. Elena and Isha have pressed questions without pushing a vote, and Priya's pressure on my silence was fair.

Omar, here is my question: if Maya is the only player with a fact-level problem on the board, does anything in the discussion give you a reason to vote for someone else today?

Noah, Maya is not the only player with a factual error: Leo incorrectly claimed she deflected my criticism after I spoke. That matters, and I won't assume his error was careless while treating hers as intentional.

Maya remains my primary suspicion because her false claim that Theo offered no answers was used directly to bolster her case against him. But I cannot establish intent, and the discussion has become heavily concentrated on one player who cannot respond. I'll weigh Leo's error and the later pressure as well when I vote.

Noah here, my third and final speaking turn. My lean is Maya, and it rests on the record, not on tone. Theo named her, cited her first and second speeches, and asked her a direct question. Maya then told the table he offered no answers. I can't prove intent, and Maya has used her three turns, so she can't explain it. That is the only fact-level problem on the board that has been pressed into a vote case, which is why I weigh it above the thin day-one reads. Leo's claim that Maya turned a question back on Omar was wrong on turn order, which dents his case, but it misstates sequence, not what someone said. Theo's looser paraphrase of Maya was corrected in his last turn. Isha, you asked Theo whether Maya's line was deliberate or careless, and Maya can't answer that now. Would you still vote Maya if you weigh Theo's framing as the bigger distortion? Name the specific line that would move you.

Noah, directly: yes, I would still vote Maya. I weigh Maya’s “offered no answers” above Theo’s looser paraphrase because it is a checkable claim about what Theo said directly to her, and she used it to keep her vote case alive. Theo’s framing in e6 did overstate her willingness to be voted out; she said she would not complain if the vote landed on her but wanted positions on record first. That was a real distortion, and it would move me if he had not corrected it in e13 by quoting her accurately and conceding the paraphrase was loose. Since he corrected it, I do not treat it as equal to Maya’s unretracted false claim. The specific line that would move me is if “offered no answers” can be shown to mean only that Theo had not answered some narrower question of hers; but Theo’s e8 named Maya, cited her first two speeches, and asked her a direct question, so that reading does not hold. I also do not want a pure bandwagon: Leo’s turn-order error in e14 is real sloppiness, and Kenji’s “fabricating” in e18 overstates intent. But Maya remains my primary suspicion because her false record claim was the centerpiece of a vote push.

I have heard the final round, and my position has not changed: I am voting Maya today. The core fact remains that Theo named her, cited her first two speeches, and asked her a direct question; Maya then told the table he had offered no answers and used that to keep her vote case alive. She cannot respond now, so we judge the record she left. I do not treat that as proof of mafia intent, but it is the strongest concrete day-one vote case on the board.

Leo’s turn-order error in e14 is real and dents his credibility. But it was a side point in his case, and it does not erase Maya’s misstatement. Kenji’s use of “fabricating” overstates what the record proves; Omar and Noah are right to separate a false statement from proof of intent. Theo’s looser paraphrase was also real, but he corrected it and quoted Maya accurately afterward, which weighs in his favor.

I will not support a late pivot to Leo based only on sloppiness. If there is a concrete case against someone other than Maya, Leo, or Theo, it needed to be on the record before this point. Otherwise, Maya remains my vote.

I want to close my read before we go to votes. My position hasn't changed: Maya is my primary suspicion, and the core of it remains her claim that Theo "offered no answers." Theo named her, cited her first two speeches, and asked her a direct question. She told the table he gave nothing, and she used that to keep a vote case alive. That is a checkable claim about the record that was wrong, and it is the strongest concrete item on the board. The fact that she has no turns left to explain it makes the record she left the only thing we can judge, and I'm comfortable judging it.

On the bandwagoning question Kenji raised with Omar: I don't think convergence is itself a problem. Most of us reached Maya independently by checking the transcript, and nearly everyone articulating a Maya vote has given their own reasoning rather than pointing at someone else's. That's not a bandwagon; that's a table reading the same facts. What I do want to avoid is a late pivot to Leo based only on his turn-order error. His mistake misstated sequence, not what someone said, and it was a side point in a three-part case. It dents his credibility, it doesn't create a rival case.

Where I part ways with Kenji slightly is on his word "fabricating." Omar is right that the record proves a false statement, not intent. I can live with that distinction and still vote Maya, because a wrong factual claim used to sustain elimination pressure is dangerous whether it was deliberate or careless.

Kenji, since you chose the stronger word: does your certainty that Maya fabricated the misstatement actually change how you vote compared to treating it as a careless error — and if the vote today fails to reach the threshold or ties, who do you want the table investigating first tomorrow, and on what evidence?

Priya, to answer your questions directly:

First, whether Maya's statement was deliberate fabrication or reckless reading does not change my vote today. Even if we step back from assessing intent, the objective reality is that Maya based an elimination push on a checkable falsehood about Theo's response. On Day 1, town has to hold players accountable to what is actually on the record. Allowing a player to press an elimination based on a fabricated absence of response sets a terrible precedent, whether born of scum malice or anti-town carelessness. So my vote will be on Maya.

Second, if today's vote fails to reach the threshold or results in a tie, the player I would look at closely tomorrow is Elena, with Leo as a secondary note. Elena spent several turns working hard to equate Theo's loose paraphrase with Maya's outright denial of reality, repeatedly trying to soften the focus on Maya. That kind of subtle equalization often comes from mafia seeking to prevent a partner's train or keep the field muddy without taking heat. Leo's sequence error in e14 also showed an eagerness to add unsupported grievances to an existing push, though that looks more like sloppy town tunneling than orchestrated deception.

With almost everyone having used their three speaking turns and clear consensus on the transcript, we have enough on record to proceed to the vote.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
Maya was eliminated.
Night begins.
Elena is mafia.
Kenji was eliminated.
Day 2 begins.

Day 2 starts with no role reveal on Maya and a night kill on Kenji. The unanimous Day 1 vote tells us little because everyone alive joined it; mafia could have bussed or simply ridden a town wagon. The more concrete new fact is Kenji's last speech. In e26 he said that if the vote failed or tied he would look first at Elena, because she repeatedly tried to equalize Theo's loose paraphrase with Maya's false "offered no answers" claim. The vote did not fail, but Kenji was killed anyway. That can mean mafia removed a sharp town voice, or it can be a deliberate frame of Elena. I do not want to treat it as proof, but it is the specific thread we should pull before we settle into another consensus.

Elena, directly: Kenji's e26 accused you of muddying the field by treating Theo's correction and Maya's unretracted false claim as equivalent. Do you think that accusation was unfair, and what in your Day 1 record shows you were weighing the facts rather than protecting Maya or softening the case against her? Also, who is your first mafia read today and why that person specifically? I am not asking for a general summary; answer the Kenji point.

Isha, I think Kenji’s accusation was unfair, though I understand why he questioned me. I never said Maya’s claim was true: in e9 and e11 I explicitly called it false. I argued that a false statement alone did not establish deliberate deception, and that Theo’s distortion also deserved scrutiny. In e15 I challenged Leo’s unsupported claim about Omar’s turn order for the same reason: we should apply the same standard to everyone. I ultimately voted Maya, not because I was certain of her role, but because I weighed the available cases at the vote.

My first suspicion today is Noah. In e20 Omar directly corrected him for saying Maya was the only player with a factual error. Noah acknowledged Leo’s mistake but repeatedly minimized it as merely a sequence error, even though Leo used the alleged deflection to strengthen his case against Maya. That selective distinction helped reinforce a consensus against someone who could no longer respond. It is not proof of mafia intent, and Kenji’s death does not establish anything about my alignment or Noah’s.

Noah, why should Leo’s unsupported deflection claim count for less simply because it depended on the order of speeches, when he also used it to build his case?

Elena, directly: I don't think Leo's error should count for less just because it concerned turn order. My earlier distinction was that it misstated sequence rather than what someone said, but I made that sound cleaner than it is. Leo used the deflection claim as a supporting point against Maya, so it does count against his credibility, just as Maya's claim about Theo did. The difference I still hold is one of size and centrality. Maya's false claim was the core of her push against Theo, while Leo's sequence error was one side point in a three-part case. I'm treating Leo's error as a credibility hit, not as an innocent detail and not as the central fact. On Kenji's e26 comment: I didn't see your Day 1 turns as protecting Maya. You called her claim false in e9 and e11, and you argued that a false statement alone doesn't prove intent. Kenji's accusation was a contingency for a failed or tied vote, and that didn't happen. His death tells us the mafia removed a player who had been pressing a specific line, but it doesn't establish anything about your alignment or mine. I'd avoid building a read on you from it. Going forward, I want to compare how each player treats the Maya and Theo exchange, and who has been pushing which line since the night result. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
